newsitem.title: GERMANY: Veba plans expansion of telecoms business.
newsitem.headline: Veba plans expansion of telecoms business.

text.p: German diversified group Veba AG said on Wednesday that it plans to dramatically expand its telecommunications business and forecast a doubling of the telecoms market after the year 2000.

Veba is one of Germany's biggest companies with 123,400 employees in September. It also reported sales of 55.3 billion marks ($36.2 billion) and group net profit of 1.227 billion marks in the first nine months of 1996.
However, in the telecommunications market it sees itself trailing behind Deutsche Telekom.

"Deutsche Telekom will be the market leader for decades in its relevant sectors of business and it's going to be tough for us to break into their market share," Veba chief executive Ulrich Hartmann told newspaper Handelsblatt in an interview.

"But like David against Goliath, we're not afraid of Deutsche Telekom," Hartmann said, adding that Veba planned to create 15,000 jobs in coming years, mainly in its telecoms sector, where it plans to add 10,000 jobs.
A Veba spokeswoman said the remaining jobs would come in its distribution and services sector.

Veba has been busy expanding its telecoms interests in recent months. It already has a partnership with Cable & Wireless and is applying the pressure to sort out its contract with fellow diversified utility RWE.
RWE took the markets by surprise recently when it pulled out of its telecoms agreement with British Telecom and Viag and instead opted to join the Veba/C&W telecoms alliance.
Hartmann denied market speculation that discussions with Veba's old rival RWE could lead to the two companies merging.

"Size in itself is not necessarily an advantage. Our telecoms joint venture with RWE is not the start of a merger. But it is true that there are no personal rivalries between management at the two companies any more," said Hartmann.
Hartmann said that the company would generate half of its turnover abroad after the year 2000, compared to nearly 30 percent today.
The reorganisation of the company's portfolio would continue and Hartmann said that Veba's units would strive to be the best in their respective activities.
He also said that while the group was planning to expand its services sector, it would seek to maintain its production basis.
Hartmann said that the group was not planning to separate itself from its oil subsidiary Veba Oil, answering market speculation that the group would be divested into a holding unit.
Veba was one of the first Germany companies to adopt principles of shareholder value, which has become a controversial term as its critics say it favours return on equity over job creation.
"It really annoys me the way in which shareholder value is discussed in Germany, because the idea of treating your shareholders fairly is clearly viewed as offensive here," said Hartmann.
Hartmann would not comment on whether or not Veba would see a dividend increase in full-year 1996. ($1=1.5255 Mark)
